vignette:
**Patient Vignette: Dr. L.**

Dr. L. is a 51-year-old married dentist of South Eastern Asian descent, who presents with a composed, almost clinical demeanor that belies the tremor in her hands when she reaches for the water glass on the corner of my desk. She has been in private practice for twenty-three years, a meticulous professional known for her steady hands and calm chairside manner.

The story she tells begins eighteen months ago. A patient, a man in his late forties whom she had treated for a routine crown, began to linger after appointments. At first, Dr. L. dismissed it as social awkwardness. He started requesting cleanings every three months instead of six. He would compliment her jewelry, remember her children’s names from a photo on her desk, and once brought her a box of expensive chocolates “for being so gentle.” She felt a prickle of unease but told herself she was being paranoid.

Then the letters began. Handwritten, left under the windshield wiper of her car. He described what she wore to work each day. He knew her route home. He wrote that her hands were the most beautiful he had ever seen and that he dreamed of them touching him. Dr. L. felt her stomach drop each time she found one. She started parking in a different lot, then on a different street. She told her husband, a quiet accountant, who offered to drive her. She declined, not wanting to disrupt his schedule.

The stalking escalated over five months. He began appearing at the grocery store she visited on Saturdays. He left a voicemail on her office line, whispering her name. He sent a letter to her home address—he had looked up her property records. Dr. L. felt her world shrinking. She stopped going to the gym. She stopped walking the dog alone. She installed a security system, but the chime of the doorbell now makes her flinch.

She finally filed a police report. A restraining order was granted. The man was arrested for violating it once, spent a weekend in jail, and has not contacted her for eleven months. The legal threat is gone. But Dr. L. says the threat is still inside her.

In her office now, she cannot face the waiting room. She has her receptionist screen all new patients, and she refuses to treat any man who is tall, with a receding hairline—a description that matches her stalker. She finds herself scanning faces in the dental chair, her peripheral vision hypervigilant. Twice in the past month, she has dropped a handpiece mid-procedure because a patient shifted suddenly in the chair, triggering a full-body startle. She apologized, blamed the light, but her heart hammered against her ribs for the rest of the appointment.

At home, she sleeps in her clothes. She cannot tolerate her husband touching her from behind. She has stopped wearing her wedding rings because the sensation of metal on her fingers reminds her of the letters describing her hands. She describes a persistent, low-grade dread, as if she is waiting for the other shoe to drop. She cannot remember the last time she felt safe in her own skin.

Dr. L. tells me this story in a flat, controlled voice, her eyes fixed on a point just above my left shoulder. She is a woman who has spent her life fixing things—cavities, cracks, broken teeth. She is deeply ashamed that she cannot fix this. She came to therapy not because she feels ready, but because she is terrified that her vigilance will one day cause her to hurt a patient. She says, with a hollow laugh, “I’m supposed to be the one who keeps people calm. Now I’m the one who’s shaking.”
